title: What Defiles, and Crumbs for the Nations
summary: Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem challenge Jesus because his disciples eat without the ritual handwashing of tradition, and he answers that they break God's command to keep their traditions and that defilement comes from the heart. In the region of Tyre and Sidon a Canaanite woman persists in asking for her daughter's healing until Jesus praises her great faith. Back by the Sea of Galilee he heals many on a mountain and feeds four thousand men, besides women and children.
story:
Jesus' reputation has now reached Jerusalem, the center of religious authority, and a delegation comes north to question him. The conflict moves from the Sabbath (chapter 12) to purity and tradition, and Jesus' answer goes to the root of the matter, the heart. Then, as if to act out what he has just taught about clean and unclean, he withdraws toward Gentile territory and meets a woman whose ancestry made her doubly an outsider. Her faith is the second example in Matthew, after the centurion in chapter 8, of a Gentile whose trust outstrips that of Israel's leaders, and her great faith stands just one chapter after Peter's little faith on the water (14:31).

The chapter belongs to the section that asks who Jesus is (13:54-16:20). The woman gives an answer: “Lord, Son of David” (verse 22). The crowds by the lake give another when they glorify the God of Israel for the healing of the lame, the blind, and the mute (verse 31). The second feeding shows that the bread of the kingdom is abundant enough for more than one table, and Jesus will recall both feedings when his disciples still fail to understand (16:9-10).
historical:
The tradition of the elders (verse 2) was the body of teaching the Pharisees had developed to apply the law of Moses to daily life. Josephus says the Pharisees passed on to the people regulations handed down by former generations that were not written in the laws of Moses, and that the Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy, rejected them (Antiquities 13.297; compare Jewish War 2.162-166); Paul, a former Pharisee, calls it ‘the traditions of my fathers’ (Galatians 1:14). Much of this oral tradition was later written down in the Mishnah, compiled under Rabbi Judah the Prince around AD 200. The Mishnah has a whole tractate on handwashing (Yadayim) and records that hands were washed before eating ordinary food as well as holy food (m. Hagigah 2:5); it preserves a dispute between the schools of Shammai and Hillel, active before AD 70, over the order of washing the hands and mixing the cup at a meal (m. Berakhot 8:2), which shows the practice already being debated in Jesus' generation. The Torah required washing of hands and feet only of priests before they served at the altar (Exodus 30:17-21). Yair Furstenberg (New Testament Studies, 2008) has argued that washing before ordinary meals was a recent Pharisaic development, based on the idea that impurity could pass from unwashed hands into food and so into the body, and that Jesus' saying in verse 11 answers exactly that idea. That scribes and Pharisees came from Jerusalem signals an official inquiry, as in Mark 3:22.

The vow in verses 5 and 6 is the one Mark 7:11 calls Corban, the Hebrew word for an offering. The Mishnah's tractate Nedarim deals with vows that dedicated property to God or forbade someone to benefit from it, and it tells of a man in Beth Horon whose father was barred by vow from benefiting from him (m. Nedarim 5:6); the same tractate records that the sages came to allow such a vow to be released when it dishonored a person's parents (m. Nedarim 9:1), so later rabbinic law moved toward Jesus' position. An ossuary lid from Jebel Hallet et-Turi near Jerusalem, published by Joseph Fitzmyer in 1959, carries the word qorban in Aramaic, the same formula in stone.

Tyre and Sidon were the old Phoenician port cities on the coast north of Galilee, rich from trade and purple dye. Tyre's silver shekel was so reliable that it became the coin of the temple tax, yet Josephus calls the Tyrians among the people most hostile to the Jews (Against Apion 1.70) and records that they killed or imprisoned many Jews in their city at the outbreak of the war in AD 66 (Jewish War 2.478). Gerd Theissen (The Gospels in Context, 1991) read the story of the woman against the tension between the wealthy Greek-speaking city and the Jewish countryside whose grain it bought. Matthew says the woman ‘came out’ from that region (verse 22), which may mean that Jesus stayed near the border rather than entering the cities themselves.

Mark calls her ‘a Greek, Syrophoenician by birth’ (Mark 7:26); Matthew calls her a Canaanite, the only use of the word in the New Testament. The name was old but not merely literary. Genesis makes Sidon the firstborn of Canaan (Genesis 10:15), Isaiah's oracle against Tyre speaks of “the strongholds of Canaan” (Isaiah 23:11), and the Phoenicians' own name for their homeland was Canaan. Augustine, centuries later, reports that Punic-speaking country people near Hippo called themselves Chanani (Unfinished Commentary on Romans 13), though Josephine Quinn has argued that the passage has been misread. Magadan (verse 39) is otherwise unknown; later manuscripts read Magdala, the fishing town on the western shore, and Mark 8:10 names Dalmanutha, equally unknown.
cultural:
Purity in Jewish life marked the line between common and holy. Impurity, contracted through contact with a corpse, certain skin diseases, bodily discharges, and some animals (Leviticus 11 to 15; Numbers 19), barred a person from the sanctuary until it was removed by time, washing, and sometimes sacrifice. It was not sin, and it was often unavoidable. The Pharisees sought to carry the purity expected of priests into ordinary meals, so that all Israel might live as a kingdom of priests (Exodus 19:6). Their washing was about ritual purity, not hygiene, and it was a serious attempt to bring God's holiness into daily life. Jesus' quarrel is with the order of priorities, not with seriousness. For Jesus to say that what enters the mouth does not defile struck near a central marker of Jewish identity; Mark draws the conclusion that he declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), while Matthew ends the discussion where it began, with unwashed hands (verse 20).

The duty to parents was grave. The fifth commandment (Exodus 20:12) was understood to include feeding, clothing, and caring for parents in old age, and the law's sanction for cursing a parent was death (Exodus 21:17), both quoted in verse 4. A son could declare property dedicated to God, a gift, and so bar his parents from benefiting from it while he might go on using it himself until it was delivered. Vows were taken with great seriousness because of Numbers 30:2, which requires a man to keep his word. Jesus treats such a vow as a way of using a religious act to escape a moral duty.

The word hypocrite (hupokritēs, verse 7) first meant a stage actor, one who speaks behind a mask, and in Matthew it names religious performance that honors God with the lips while the heart is elsewhere. Blind guides (verse 14) was a pointed image: Paul describes a Jewish teacher confident that he is a guide to the blind (Romans 2:19), and Jesus turns the phrase on the Pharisees here and in 23:16 and 24. The picture of Israel as God's planting (verse 13) was well known: Isaiah calls the restored people the branch of God's planting (Isaiah 60:21) and oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord (Isaiah 61:3); the Qumran community called itself an eternal planting (1QS 8:5), and 1 Enoch speaks of the plant of righteousness (1 Enoch 10:16). Jesus says that whatever God did not plant will be uprooted.

Dogs in the Bible are mostly scavengers of the street, unclean and despised (1 Kings 21:23, Psalm 22:16), and dog could be an insult (1 Samuel 17:43; later Philippians 3:2). Jesus uses the diminutive kunarion, and the woman takes up the picture of little dogs under a family table. Whether the diminutive softens the word is debated. Many grammarians note that diminutives in the Greek of the period had often lost their force, while N. Clayton Croy (New Testament Studies, 2024) has argued that kunarion keeps a real sense of small or household dog. The children in the saying are Israel, whom God called his son (Exodus 4:22), and the table is God's provision for his people. The woman's cry, ‘Have mercy on me, Lord’, uses the words that became the church's Kyrie eleison, and her kneeling (verse 25) is the same verb Matthew uses for worship. For the second feeding, the seven baskets (spuris) are a different word from the twelve of 14:20; a spuris could be large enough to hold a man, since Paul was let down the wall of Damascus in one (Acts 9:25).
literary:
Matthew follows Mark 7:1-8:10 but reshapes it. He drops Mark's long explanation of Jewish washings (Mark 7:3-4), which his readers presumably did not need. He reverses the order of Jesus' reply, so that Jesus answers the charge of breaking tradition with a counter-charge of breaking God's command (verse 3) before quoting Isaiah (verses 8 and 9), a sharper and more lawyerly structure. He omits Mark's comment that Jesus declared all foods clean and ends with a verdict on handwashing alone (verse 20). He adds verses 12 to 14, where the disciples report that the Pharisees were offended and Jesus answers with the sayings about the plant and the blind guides, and he has Peter, not the disciples in general, ask for the explanation (verse 15), one of several places where Matthew gives Peter a voice.

The controversy is built in three scenes, each to a different audience: the leaders (verses 1 to 9), the crowd (verses 10 and 11), and the disciples (verses 12 to 20). Jesus' answer turns on two sayings set side by side, “God said” (verse 4) and “But you say” (verse 5), and it quotes Isaiah 29:13 in a form close to the Greek Old Testament, whose last line, teaching as doctrines the precepts of men, fits the argument more sharply than the Hebrew. The list in verse 19 is shorter than Mark's thirteen and ordered differently: after evil thoughts come murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander, which follow the sequence of the sixth to ninth commandments (Exodus 20:13-16), with sexual immorality beside adultery and slander after false witness. Jesus moves from the table to the Ten Commandments, from what touches the hands to what comes from the heart.

The Canaanite woman's story is built on four obstacles, three of them added by Matthew: Jesus' silence, the disciples' request to send her away, and his statement “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (verse 24), before the saying about the dogs that Matthew shares with Mark. Each is met by her persistence, and the scene turns on her reply. Matthew omits Mark's ‘first’ (Mark 7:27), which makes the saying sound harsher, and replaces Mark's ‘because of this answer’ with “your faith is great”. The feeding of the four thousand (verses 32 to 39) is told with deliberate echoes of the five thousand in chapter 14, and the mountain of verse 29, where Jesus sits as he sat to teach in 5:1, gathers the healings into a picture of Isaiah 35:5-6, where the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, and the mute shout for joy.

outline.t: The tradition of the elders and the command of God
Many healed by the Sea of Galilee

doctrines.note: Jesus distinguishes the commandment of God from human tradition and refuses to let the second overrule the first (verses 3 to 6), treating the written law as God's word by which every tradition is judged. Matthew, who insists that Jesus came to fulfill the law (5:17), ends the argument with handwashing (verse 20) and does not repeat Mark's comment about foods; Christians differ on how far verse 11 reaches beyond that question (see the second hard question).

Jesus locates the source of evil not in outside contamination but in the human heart, from which come evil thoughts and the breaking of the commandments (verses 18 and 19). No washing reaches the place where evil begins, and worship offered with the lips while the heart is far away is empty (verse 8).

The case Jesus chooses concerns the family. The fifth commandment binds children to honor and support their parents, and a vow that frees a son from that duty nullifies the word of God (verses 4 to 6). Care for aging parents belongs to the worship God commands, and no gift to God can be paid with what is owed to them.

Jesus says he was sent “only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (verse 24), echoing his charge to the Twelve (10:5-6), yet he heals a Canaanite's daughter, and the risen Jesus will send the disciples to all nations (28:19). The chapter holds Israel's priority and the nations' inclusion together, as God's promise to Abraham did (Genesis 12:3).

The Canaanite woman's faith is humble, persistent, and sharp. She calls Jesus Lord and Son of David, kneels, accepts the picture of the table, and trusts that even crumbs from it are enough. Jesus calls her faith great (verse 28), words he uses of no one else in Matthew, though he marveled at the Gentile centurion's faith (8:10), and they stand in contrast to the disciples' little faith (14:31, 16:8).

words.note: Paradosis, tradition, literally something handed over. It occurs 13 times in the New Testament, three in this chapter and five in Mark 7. It can be good: Paul commends the traditions he handed on (1 Corinthians 11:2, 2 Thessalonians 2:15). It can be bad, when human additions override God's command, as here and in Colossians 2:8. The question in verse 3 is not tradition as such but its authority relative to God's word.

Hupokritēs, hypocrite. In ordinary Greek it meant an actor, one who plays a part on stage. It occurs 18 times in the New Testament, most of them in Matthew (thirteen or fourteen, depending on whether 23:14 is counted), and Jesus uses it of religious performance: giving, praying, and fasting to be seen (6:2, 5, 16), and here honoring God with the lips while the heart is far away (verse 7). BDAG notes that in biblical Greek it takes on the sense of one who is godless under a pious mask.

Koinoō, to make common, defile. In Jewish usage common (koinos) meant not set apart as holy, and so ritually unclean, a sense rare in secular Greek. The verb occurs 14 times in the New Testament, five here (verse 11 twice, 18, and 20 twice), five in Mark 7, and three in Acts, including Peter's vision (Acts 10:15, 11:9). Jesus uses it to relocate defilement: what comes out of the heart makes a person unclean before God.

Hodēgos, guide, one who leads the way. It occurs five times in the New Testament: here, twice in the woes against the scribes and Pharisees (23:16, 24), of Judas as a guide to those who arrested Jesus (Acts 1:16), and in Paul's description of a teacher sure he is ‘a guide for the blind’ (Romans 2:19). Blind guides is Matthew's recurring charge against leaders who claim to lead others to God while unable to see him themselves.

Chananaios, Canaanite. It occurs only here in the New Testament. In the Greek Old Testament it names the peoples of the land Israel entered (for example Genesis 12:6), whom Israel was told to drive out. By choosing this old name rather than Mark's Syrophoenician, Matthew underlines how far outside Israel she stands, and his readers may remember that the Messiah's own genealogy includes the Canaanite Rahab (1:5).

Eleeō, to have mercy, show compassion. It occurs 32 times in the New Testament, eight in Matthew. The cry ‘have mercy on me’ is the language of the Psalms (Psalm 51:1), and in Matthew it is the cry of the needy to the Son of David (9:27, 20:30-31) as well as of this woman (verse 22) and a father (17:15). The Greek Kyrie eleison, ‘Lord, have mercy’, became a fixed part of Christian liturgy, East and West.

Kunarion, little dog or house dog, the diminutive of kuōn, dog. It occurs only four times in the New Testament, all in this story and its parallel (verses 26 and 27; Mark 7:27-28). Whether the diminutive softens the saying is debated (see the cultural note), but the woman seizes on the picture of dogs that belong to a household and eat under its table, and turns Jesus' words into her plea.

Spuris, basket or hamper. It occurs five times in the New Testament: in the second feeding (verse 37; Mark 8:8) and the later recollections of it (16:10, Mark 8:20), and for the basket in which Paul was lowered over the Damascus wall (Acts 9:25). The first feeding uses kophinos (14:20, 16:9), and Jesus' question in 16:9-10 keeps the two words distinct, a sign that the Gospels remember two separate meals.

christ:
Jesus speaks in the first half as the one who can tell God's will from human additions and read the law at its deepest intent. The prophets had rebuked worship without the heart (Isaiah 29:13, Hosea 6:6), and Jesus takes up Isaiah's words with his own authority and declares what truly defiles. He does not set aside the commandment to honor parents; he defends it against those who evade it. The one who will later say that not a stroke of the law will pass away (5:18) shows here what fulfilling the law looks like: a heart made clean, from which obedience comes.

The Canaanite woman gives Jesus the titles of Israel's king, Lord and Son of David, and he acts as Israel's Messiah whose blessing reaches the nations. God had promised Abraham that “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3), and Jesus had already said that many will come from east and west to share the banquet with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (8:11). His statement that he was sent to the lost sheep of Israel recalls God's promise to shepherd his scattered flock himself (Ezekiel 34:11-16) and Jeremiah's lament, “My people are lost sheep” (Jeremiah 50:6). The shepherd comes first to Israel, but a Gentile mother's faith already receives what the risen Christ will send his disciples to bring to all nations (28:19).

On the mountain by the lake the healings echo Isaiah 35, where God comes to save and “the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped” and “the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:5-6), and the crowds glorify the God of Israel. The second feeding shows the Shepherd again providing bread in the wilderness, moved by compassion as before (verse 32; 14:14), and the pattern of taking, giving thanks, breaking, and giving (verse 36) points to the Last Supper, where he will give thanks over the cup (26:27). The one who feeds Israel's children also lets the crumbs fall.
interpretation:
Jewish readers have long recognized the debate of verses 1 to 11 as an argument within Judaism. The Mishnah's rulings on handwashing and on releasing vows made against parents (m. Nedarim 9:1) show the same questions among the sages, and a later saying attributed to Yohanan ben Zakkai holds that a corpse does not in itself defile nor water purify, but that the ritual is a decree of God which Israel may not transgress (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 4:7), keeping the practice while granting its inner meaning. Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012) argues that the Jesus of Mark 7 defends the written Torah against newer Pharisaic rules, and Matthew's ending at handwashing (verse 20) has made that reading especially attractive for this chapter. Amy-Jill Levine's study of Matthew's salvation history (The Social and Ethnic Dimensions of Matthean Salvation History, 1988) examined how the Gospel moves from the mission to Israel alone (10:5-6, 15:24) to the mission to all nations (28:19).

The church fathers read the Canaanite woman as a figure of the Gentile church. Origen's Commentary on Matthew (book 11) discussed both the Corban vow and the woman at length. Hilary of Poitiers (Commentary on Matthew, around 355) read her daughter as the Gentile peoples held by unclean spirits. Augustine (Sermon 77) praised her humility: called a dog, she did not deny it, and so received what she asked, a figure of the Gentiles grafted in through humility. John Chrysostom read Jesus' silence and refusals as a way of drawing out and displaying her faith. The Didache (9:5), an early church manual, applied Jesus' separate saying about not giving what is holy to dogs (7:6) to the Eucharist, a sign of how early the image of the table was read of the Lord's Supper.

The historic Western lectionary read 15:21-28 on the Second Sunday in Lent (Reminiscere), and it drew some of the Reformation's most memorable preaching. Luther's sermon on the text (1525) says she catches Christ in his own words: granting that she is a dog, she asks only what a dog is allowed, the crumbs, and so holds him to his own verdict, a picture of faith that clings to God's word even when God seems to say no. Thomas Cranmer drew on the same scene for the Prayer of Humble Access in the Order of the Communion (1548), carried into the Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1552, 1662), in which communicants confess that they are not worthy even to gather the crumbs under the Lord's table. The Reformers also used verses 3 to 9 against human traditions in worship, while Catholic writers answered that apostolic tradition, which Paul commends (2 Thessalonians 2:15), is not what Jesus condemns.

Modern readers have argued most over the woman. Feminist interpreters, beginning with Sharon Ringe's essay on the Markan story (1985), read her as the one who teaches Jesus; Musa Dube (Postcolonial Feminist Interpretation of the Bible, 2000) read Matthew's Canaanite woman through the story of Rahab and saw in the scene the voice of a colonized people. Others, including many evangelical and Catholic commentators, read the scene as a test that reveals her faith. On the four thousand, J. R. C. Cousland (Novum Testamentum, 1999) questioned the argument that praising the God of Israel proves the crowd Jewish, and a later study in the Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society (2020) argued that Matthew means a Gentile crowd; others hold that Matthew, who drops Mark's reference to the Decapolis, pictures Israel. The Revised Common Lectionary reads 15:(10-20) 21-28 on Proper 15 in Year A, and the Roman lectionary reads 15:21-28 on the Twentieth Sunday in Ordinary Time. Jean-Germain Drouais's The Woman of Canaan at the Feet of Christ (1784), now in the Louvre, won the Prix de Rome.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles in this chapter come from manuscripts. In verse 6 the earliest witnesses, including Codex Sinaiticus as corrected and Codex Vaticanus, read that the Pharisees nullify “the word of God”; a few early witnesses read ‘the law of God’, and the later manuscripts behind the King James Version read ‘the commandment of God’, which matches verse 3. In the same verse some early manuscripts have only ‘his father’, while others add ‘or his mother’, as in verse 5. In verse 4 the King James Version's ‘God commanded, saying’ follows later manuscripts, where the earliest read simply that God said. In verse 8 the King James Version begins, ‘This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth’, words found in the Greek Old Testament of Isaiah 29:13 and added to Matthew in later manuscripts; the earliest witnesses have the shorter form the BSB translates.

In verse 14 many manuscripts read ‘blind guides of the blind’ (KJV, ‘blind leaders of the blind’), while some early witnesses have simply ‘blind guides’. In verses 30 and 31 the manuscripts list the lame, blind, crippled, and mute in several different orders, a common kind of scribal variation that does not affect the sense. In verse 39 the earliest witnesses read Magadan, an otherwise unknown place, while later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read Magdala, the better-known town on the lake; Mark 8:10 has Dalmanutha. In verse 26 translations differ over whether to render kunarion as ‘dogs’ (KJV, ESV, BSB) or ‘little dogs’ (NKJV), a choice that reflects the debate over the diminutive.

teach.big: What makes a person unclean before God is not what touches the hands but what comes from the heart, and the Jesus who exposes the heart is the Son of David who extends mercy to a Canaanite mother and bread to the crowds.

outline.t: God's word judges every tradition, and a tradition that lets us look devout while neglecting the people God gave us to care for has turned worship into performance.
Defilement starts inside: the heart, not the hands or the menu, is where evil is born, and only a cleansing that reaches the heart can make us clean.
Faith accepts the truth about itself, holds Jesus to his own words, and keeps asking through silence and refusal, trusting that a crumb of his mercy is enough.
When Jesus comes, Isaiah's promise is seen: the broken are made whole, and the watching crowds give glory to the God of Israel.
Jesus' compassion does not run out after one miracle; he feeds again, and his disciples must learn not to forget what he has already done.

teach.pitfalls:
The first misreading turns the Pharisees into cartoons of legalism. Their purity practice was a serious attempt to make all of life holy, and many of their own teachers agreed with Jesus about vows against parents. Preaching that sneers at them misses the point, which is that devout people of every age, churchgoers included, can let their traditions override God's command. The second pitfall is to conclude that tradition as such is bad. Jesus judges traditions by God's word; he does not reject the handing on of the faith, which Paul commends. A third error reads verses 10 to 20 as permission to treat outward conduct as unimportant, as if the body and behavior did not matter so long as the heart is right. Jesus' list is a list of commandments broken in deed, and the heart is where they begin, not where they end.

With the Canaanite woman, avoid two easy versions. One makes Jesus' refusals a staged test with a wink, as if nothing in his words were hard; the other makes the scene proof that Jesus was a bigot corrected by a woman. Matthew supports neither: the words are hard, the order of Israel first is real in his Gospel (10:5-6), and the outcome is praise for her great faith. Do not use the scene to paint first-century Judaism as the source of ethnic contempt; the saying is on Jesus' lips, and Matthew's point is where the story lands. Finally, avoid reading the second feeding as a mere duplicate of the first, or loading its numbers with codes Matthew does not supply.
teach.pastoral: The chapter can press hard on people raised in religious systems that measured holiness by outward conformity, and on those who carry shame from being treated as unclean because of their background, ethnicity, divorce, or past. Teach verses 10 to 20 as release from a false standard, not as a new burden of introspection; people prone to scrupulosity may hear the list of evils from the heart as an accusation they can never escape, and they need to hear that Jesus answers the heart's defilement with mercy. The Corban example touches families strained by the care of aging parents; some will feel guilt for not doing more and others resentment at duties they cannot sustain. The text condemns evasion by religious excuse, not the real limits of caregivers. Parents of sick or troubled children will hear the Canaanite mother's persistence with special force. Some in the room have prayed through long silence; they should hear both that silence is not the last word in this story and that Jesus answered her.

hard.q: Why does Jesus ignore the Canaanite woman, say he was sent only to Israel, and compare her to a dog?
hard.a:
The objection is sharper in Matthew than in Mark. Matthew adds Jesus' silence (verse 23), his agreement in effect with the disciples' wish to be rid of her, and the flat statement “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (verse 24), and he omits Mark's word ‘first’ (Mark 7:27), which softens the saying in Mark by implying that Gentiles will be fed later. What remains is a desperate mother refused with a proverb that likens her people to dogs, a word used in Scripture and later Jewish writing for the despised. Sharon Ringe (1985) called the Markan reply flippant and even cruel and argued that the woman corrects Jesus. Musa Dube (Postcolonial Feminist Interpretation of the Bible, 2000) read Matthew's scene as the voice of a conquered people, recalling the Canaanites of Joshua, who must accept the label dog to receive anything. Skeptical readers take the saying as evidence that the historical Jesus shared the ethnic prejudices of his time, which the church later softened. Jewish readers have noted, with justice, that Christian commentators often explain the saying away by blaming Jewish attitudes, when the words are on Jesus' own lips.

Responses take several forms. Many interpreters from John Chrysostom and Augustine (Sermon 77) onward read the silence and refusals as a test that draws out and displays her faith, and Luther's sermon on the text (1525) pictured her catching Christ in his own words, holding him to the place he assigned her and asking only what that place allows. A second line stresses salvation history. Jesus' earthly mission in Matthew was genuinely directed to Israel first (10:5-6), and the move to all nations comes after the resurrection (28:19); Amy-Jill Levine (1988) has shown how carefully Matthew structures that sequence. On this view the saying states an order, not a verdict on her worth, and her faith anticipates the order's fulfillment. Some add that the diminutive kunarion, which N. Clayton Croy (2024) argues means household dogs, and the picture of a family table leave room for her reply, though Croy's argument leans on Mark's ‘first’, which Matthew lacks. A third line, taken by Ringe and others, holds that Jesus in his real humanity came to a wider view through the encounter; others answer that nothing in Matthew shows him changing his mind, only granting her request on the ground of her faith. What is not in dispute is the outcome: Jesus praises her faith as great, words he uses of no one else in Matthew, heals her daughter at once, and in Matthew's arrangement the scene answers the question about clean and unclean that opens the chapter. Readers need not smooth over the harshness to see where the story lands.

hard.q: Does verse 11 abolish the Jewish food laws, and why does Matthew not say so as Mark does?
hard.a:
The objection has two forms. Jewish scholars such as Daniel Boyarin (The Jewish Gospels, 2012), with Christian scholars such as James Crossley (The Date of Mark's Gospel, 2004), argue that neither the historical Jesus nor the Gospel writers set aside the Torah's food laws: the dispute concerns handwashing, a Pharisaic tradition, not the biblical laws of Leviticus 11, and Matthew makes this explicit by ending with “eating with unwashed hands does not defile him” (verse 20). On this view, reading verse 11 as the end of the food laws makes Jesus contradict Matthew 5:17-19, where not a stroke of the law will pass away. Many scholars of Matthew's setting, among them J. Andrew Overman (1990) and Anthony Saldarini (Matthew's Christian-Jewish Community, 1994), read the Gospel as the work of a law-observant community of Jewish believers. Skeptical readers press the point from the other side: if Jesus had declared all foods clean, as Mark 7:19 says, why did Peter need a vision before eating with Gentiles (Acts 10:9-16), why did the church at Antioch divide over table fellowship (Galatians 2:11-14), and why does Matthew, retelling this scene, leave Mark's comment out?

Responses begin with Matthew's own words. His Jesus speaks about what defiles a person before God, and verse 11 states a principle about the heart that is broader than the handwashing question which occasioned it. Some readers hold that Matthew deliberately limits the application to handwashing because his community still kept the food laws, and that the principle's fuller reach was drawn out later, as Mark's comment and Paul's conviction that “nothing is unclean in itself” (Romans 14:14) show. Others hold that Jesus relativized ritual purity without abolishing it, teaching, as the prophets did, that moral defilement matters more (Hosea 6:6, which Matthew quotes twice, 9:13 and 12:7), and that the church came to the full conclusion under the Spirit's guidance (Acts 15:28-29). On either view the delay seen in Acts is what one would expect if a principle stated about the heart took years to be worked out at the table, and the Gospels do not claim that the disciples understood it at the time (verse 16). Christians have held these readings side by side, and how Jesus' own practice related to Mark's comment remains an open question among interpreters of every tradition.

observe: What charge do the Pharisees and scribes bring in verse 2, and with what counter-charge and example does Jesus answer in verses 3 to 6?
What four obstacles does the Canaanite woman meet, and how does she respond to each?
What does the crowd see on the mountain in verses 30 and 31, and whom do they glorify?
interpret: Why does Jesus say that what comes out of the mouth defiles a person rather than what goes in, and how does the list in verse 19 connect to the commandments?
How do Jesus' words “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” fit with his healing of her daughter and with the command to make disciples of all nations (28:19)?
Why might Matthew place the healing of a Canaanite's daughter immediately after Jesus' teaching on clean and unclean?
apply: Jesus accused the Pharisees of honoring God with their lips while their hearts were far away. Where might that describe your own worship?
What traditions, good in themselves, have you seen become more important than love for God or for the people God has given you to care for, including aging parents?
The Canaanite woman kept asking through silence and refusal. What does her persistence teach you about praying when God seems silent?
